correctness.rationale: In a matched three-point support, a collision between distinct nonzero ordered differences either reverses a pair (impossible at odd p) or makes one point the midpoint of the other two. Hence the nonempty overlap sizes are 3,2,2,1,1 for a progression and 3,1,1,1,1,1,1 otherwise. The five progression shifts are distinct even at p=5, where the nonprogression case cannot occur. Prime Fourier uncertainty bounds the row zeros by overlap size minus one. For a nonprogression, the kernel of the two selected central Fourier rows is generated by signed minors, all nonzero, so the two exact zeros are attained, with every side row a monomial. For a progression, the side-row root ratios multiply to the constant-to-leading coefficient ratio of the center quadratic, yielding the resonance by Vieta. Conversely, choose central coefficients (γδ,−(γ+δ),1), take G_1=G_2=1, choose conjugate(G_0)=α/(γ+δ), and choose F_0 so F_0 conjugate(G_0)=γδ. The middle and last signal coefficients are −(γ+δ),1. Then the upper side root is α and the lower side root is γδ/α. None of the factors vanish at odd p, and all specified zeros are the only ones in their rows. The frequency dilation is bijective, so the pattern counts follow. The uploaded exact cyclotomic checker for p=5,7,11,13 was inspected, not executed.

originality.rationale: The progression minimum and the Vieta constraint are explicitly covered for p≥7 by Resultary 9566ceddf117, which treats arbitrary three-tap pairs and has an exact coefficient-level characterization of the five-row regime. Realizing a designated permissible root tuple amounts to solving the displayed coefficient ratios. The remaining nonprogression minimum and all its patterns follow directly from the cited prime Fourier support realization theorem, because all noncentral rows are monomials. The small p=5 progression case uses the same five-row formulas without the need for inverse support geometry. This is demonstrated coverage and implication, not a claim about which indexed record came first.
